extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate courts, and practitioners addressing §101 challenges for computer-implemented inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and judicial criteria for assessing patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), with emphasis on computer-implemented inventions, how to treat claim language, and when §101 can be resolved on the pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit §101 exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implicit exception reflects the concern that patent law must not 'improperly tying up the future use of' building blocks of human ingenuity (quoting Mayo/ Alice / Myriad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step Alice/Mayo framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea). Step 2: Consider the elements of each claim both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether the additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Mayo and Alice as articulated by the Supreme Court; step-one asks what the claim is 'directed to' and step-two asks if there's something 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the claim 'as a whole' and the claimed advance
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one courts must evaluate the claim's character 'as a whole' and assess 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine if the claim is directed to excluded subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not improperly dissect claims into isolated portions when determining what the claim is directed to; focus on the claim language itself to identify the claimed advance (citing Diehr, Intell. Ventures I v. Erie, ChargePoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea indicators: mental processes and pen-and-paper analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim features that are mental processes or can be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper are indicative of an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include classification, indexing, locating, collecting/recognizing data, and other human-analogous operations (citing CyberSource, Parker v. Flook, Erie, Symantec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical algorithms and information analysis are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing information by steps people go through in their minds, or by mathematical algorithms, is treated as an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generating identifiers via a known algorithm (e.g., cryptographic hash, message digest) or transforming data by an algorithm can be within the abstract-idea category (citing Elec. Power Group, RecogniCorp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting, comparing, and recognizing data is abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that collect data and recognize certain data within the collected set (for example, comparing content-based identifiers) are abstract mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symantec and Content Extraction illustrate that determining whether identifiers match or characterizing data based on identifiers constitutes an abstract idea (collecting, recognizing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-management functions can be abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions such as controlling access to data, retrieving/delivering data, and marking duplicates for deletion are mental processes and thus may be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: controlling access (library/library-card analogue), retrieving data (index/search), and discarding duplicates (classifying data) are longstanding human practices and indicative of abstraction (citing Ericsson, Erie, Symantec, Secured Mail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining multiple abstract ideas does not necessarily make a claim non-abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Stringing together abstract steps—i.e., 'adding one abstract idea to another'—generally amounts to an abstract idea when the combination simply performs the same mental processes in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A multistep mental process that combines abstract ideas remains abstract unless the combination yields something beyond mere aggregation of abstract concepts (citing RecogniCorp, Elec. Power Group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere recitation of a generic computer component (server system, generic hash function, computer performing routine tasks) does not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on computers to perform routine tasks more quickly or accurately, or using generic computer hardware/software, is insufficient; courts treat mere automation of manual processes using generic computers as failing §101 (citing OIP Techs., Intell. Ventures v. Cap. One, SAP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in computer technology versus using computers as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' and that solve problems specifically arising in computer networks may be non-abstract (DDR Holdings exception); by contrast, claims that use computers merely as tools to automate conventional human activity are abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim's focus is an improvement in computers as tools (which may weigh toward eligibility) or an independently abstract idea that merely uses computers as tools (which fails step one).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step two — inventive concept requirement ('significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, courts search for an inventive concept—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept can arise from unconventional features or improvements in technology, but must go beyond restating the abstract idea or claiming conventional computer functionality (citing Alice, Mayo, SAP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality and generic features do not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Using well-known, routine, or conventional elements (e.g., generic hash functions, standard servers, existing operating systems) does not provide the 'something more' required under step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a particular use of a technique was not widely practiced, that alone does not render an abstract idea patent-eligible; novelty of an abstract idea does not equal an inventive concept (citing SAP, PersonalWeb reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: A new abstract idea remains an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the claimed abstract idea is new or not previously known, it remains an abstract idea for §101 purposes and is not rendered patentable merely by novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly held that novelty of the abstract idea itself cannot satisfy §101 (citing SAP and Synopsys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'dissect' claims into eligible and ineligible elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not read out or ignore claim elements labeled 'abstract' when assessing the claim; Diehr instructs that claims are not to be dissected into eligible and ineligible elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At both steps, the proper analysis considers claim elements together (and as an ordered combination) rather than wholesale excising portions of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scope of the 'abstract idea' characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: When identifying the abstract idea, courts must avoid defining it too broadly (sweeping in concrete computer operations not historically deemed abstract) or too narrowly (failing to credit technical benefits and the claimed advance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mischaracterizing the abstract idea (either overbroadly or overly narrowly) can lead to incorrect conclusions; courts should credit technical benefits and focus on the claimed advance over the prior art (citing Diehr, Alice, and criticisms of Federal Circuit practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility is a legal question that may involve factual disputes (Berkheimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 is a question of law that can involve underlying questions of fact; genuine disputes of fact material to the inquiry can preclude resolution on the pleadings (per Berkheimer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every §101 determination involves genuine factual disputes; where undisputed facts permit a ruling, courts may resolve eligibility on a motion to dismiss or judgment on the pleadings (citing Simio, SAP, Berkheimer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural standard for resolving §101 on pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution of §101 on a Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c) motion is appropriate when the undisputed facts, taken as true under the motion standard, require a holding of ineligibility; procedural law of the regional circuit governs (e.g., Ninth Circuit reviews 12(c) de novo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the plausibility standard (Iqbal/Twombly) when assessing whether the complaint contains sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim of eligibility; courts may convert motions only where appropriate and must accept pleaded facts as true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification disclosures and factual questions about inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that the specification discloses improvements can create fact questions, but such disclosures must show an inventive concept in the non-abstract application realm to defeat a §101 motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification's purported improvements lie entirely in the realm of abstract ideas (and not in a non-abstract application), they do not supply an inventive concept; courts evaluate whether the specification plausibly alleges technical improvements beyond the abstract idea (citing SAP, PersonalWeb).
